chunks: "I avoid vias wherever the via's parasitics or its manufacturing risk cost more than the routing convenience it gives me. Electrically, that's fast edges and RF.
A typical via is around a nanohenry, and the reflection from that goes up as the rise time shrinks: with a 1.
3 nanohenries via on a 50 ohm line, a 100 picosecond edge reflects around 13 percent in the worst case, while a one nanosecond edge reflects about one percent.

So on multi-gigabit lanes, clocks, and RF paths I keep the signal on one layer if I can, or I limit it to as few layer changes as possible, add ground vias beside them, and use back-drilled or blind vias to kill the stub.
In differential pairs I keep both vias symmetric so I don't add skew. For manufacturing, I don't put an open via in an SMT pad, because solder wicks into it.
I also keep vias away from board edges and mounting holes, where cracking and plating exposure are a risk, and I avoid tight aspect ratios.
And for power, I avoid having just one or two vias carry current, or covering a power plane with so many vias that it turns into Swiss cheese.
In all these cases I either stay on one layer, move the via, add vias in parallel or choose a different type."
